clue.text: Small work by American in MoMA fenced off

indicators.note: something that has gone off is spoiled, so the letters before it are broken up and rearranged

blocks.note: all twelve letters are used as fodder

explanation.surface: A miniature piece by an American artist is roped off at New York's Museum of Modern Art.
explanation.walkthrough: MoMA is the Museum of Modern Art in New York, which makes 'work' look like an artwork; it is Steinbeck's short novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Of Mice and Men is a novella, a short book, by the American writer John Steinbeck.

clue.text: Professional running service at a loss?

definitions.text: Professional running service at a loss?

blocks.clueFragment: Professional running service at a loss
blocks.note: surface reading: a professional who runs a business service and is losing money
setter's reading: the service is a funeral and the loss is a bereavement

explanation.walkthrough: 'At a loss' suggests unprofitable trading, but here the loss is a death, and the service is the one held for it.
explanation.definitionFit: An undertaker is the professional who organises and conducts the ceremony after someone dies.

clue.text: Primate kept up by weird nightmare

indicators.note: what is kept by the following words is held inside them, sitting across the word break
in a down clue, going up means reading the letters from bottom to top

blocks.note: the letters straddling the two words

explanation.surface: A monkey lies awake, kept up at night by a strange bad dream.
explanation.definitionFit: The indri is a large lemur of Madagascar, and lemurs belong to the primate order.

clue.text: Swamp English boy cutting grass at the side of the road

indicators.note: a thing that cuts into another goes inside it, splitting it in two

blocks.clueFragment: grass at the side of the road
blocks.note: the grassy strip bordering a road

explanation.surface: An English boy mows the grass verge beside the road.
explanation.definitionFit: An everglade is a marshy, grassy tract of land, the type found in the Florida Everglades: a kind of swamp.

clue.text: NCO positive soldiers sit around without good reason

indicators.note: turning around faces the other way, so the word sit is read from its end

blocks.note: a non-commissioned officer, informally a noncom

explanation.surface: An army sergeant insists the troops are lounging about for no good reason.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reason' here means sanity rather than justification.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin legal phrase means not of sound mind, so lacking one's reason or sanity.

clue.text: Crime boss from Britain taken up in Putin's jet

indicators.note: in a down clue, taken up means lifted so the letters read upwards, back to front
the word in places the earlier letters inside the following word

blocks.note: the MiG is a Russian fighter plane

explanation.surface: A British gangster is flown off in a Russian president's private jet.
explanation.definitionFit: Mr Big is the slang label for the boss at the top of a criminal gang.

clue.text: Liberal bores want journalist bugged

indicators.note: something that bores drills into another thing, so it ends up inside it

explanation.surface: Tedious Lib Dems want a reporter's phone tapped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bugged' looks like phone-tapping but means annoyed.
explanation.definitionFit: To needle someone is to irritate them, so needled and bugged both mean annoyed.

clue.text: Famous lion tamer's head at an angle

indicators.note: the head of a word is its opening letter

blocks.note: the lion in C.S. Lewis's Narnia books

explanation.surface: A lion tamer's head is cocked to one side as he faces the famous beast.
explanation.definitionFit: Aslant means slanting or obliquely, lying at an angle rather than straight.

clue.text: Patronise all the locals, turning up to fight outside clubs

definitions.note: a verb phrase defining a noun answer, fair because pub-crawl is also used as a verb meaning to go on such a tour

indicators.note: turning a word around makes it read the other way
the word outside places the fight word around the clubs letter

explanation.surface: Support every neighbourhood shop, arriving to scrap outside the nightclubs.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a local is your regular pub, so to patronise all the locals is to drink in each one.
explanation.definitionFit: A pub crawl is a tour drinking in one bar after another, giving custom to each.

clue.text: Dirty EastEnder headbutts, in return getting floored

indicators.note: something given in return comes back the other way, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: Dirty Den Watts, a notorious character in the BBC soap EastEnders
to nut someone is to headbutt them

explanation.surface: A grubby Londoner headbutts someone and gets knocked flat in retaliation.
explanation.walkthrough: EastEnders is a long-running BBC soap set in east London; Dirty Den was its most famous villain, so 'Dirty' is part of his name, not a description.
explanation.definitionFit: To be floored is to be knocked down or utterly astonished, both senses of stunned.

clue.text: Sadly, none live to collect paintball's ultimate honour

indicators.note: a word sadly done is done badly, so the letters come out in a wrong order
the ultimate part of a word is its final letter
to collect something is to gather it in, so one piece is held inside another

blocks.note: to live is to be, to exist

explanation.surface: Sadly, nobody survives a paintball match to receive the top award.
explanation.definitionFit: To ennoble someone is to raise them to the peerage, a high honour, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: If you believe account, my racket got smashed

indicators.note: something smashed is broken into bits that come back together in a different order

blocks.note: a racket is a loud noise

explanation.surface: If you trust the story, my tennis racket was broken.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Racket' looks like a bat for tennis but means noise; 'Cor!' is a British exclamation like 'My!'.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying 'according to' someone reports a claim on their authority, the phrase for what you'd accept if you believe them.

clue.text: Young lady heads for gents, avoiding lines

indicators.note: the heads of a group of words are their leading letters

blocks.note: the opening letter of each word

explanation.surface: A young woman heads for the men's lavatory, skipping the queues.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gents' is British for a men's public toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: Gal is an informal word for a girl or young woman.

clue.text: Drag bed from unsightly spot over by lake

indicators.note: turning over flips the word so it reads backwards

blocks.note: a wart is an ugly growth on the skin

explanation.surface: Haul a bed out of an ugly corner beside the lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bed' here is the sea bed or river bed, not furniture.
explanation.definitionFit: To trawl is to drag a large fishing net along the sea floor.

clue.text: Power feeding alarm warning light went off quickly

indicators.note: feeding something puts it inside, as food goes into a mouth

explanation.surface: A power surge set off the alarm, and the warning light flashed on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Went off' suggests an alarm sounding, but it means ran away; scarper is British slang for flee.
explanation.definitionFit: To scarper is British slang for running away fast, so scarpered means fled or went off in a hurry.

clue.text: Veronica's son was good on the potty?

blocks.note: a toddler who has peed well has performed well on the potty

explanation.surface: A mother named Veronica reports her little boy behaved well during toilet training.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Veronica's' looks like a mother's name with a possessive, but it is the plant name plus 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Veronica is the botanical genus name for speedwell, a small blue-flowered plant.

clue.text: Turn say, northwards below clear path on hill

indicators.note: in a down clue, going northwards means reading from the bottom up, back to front
in a down entry, below places this part after the next one

blocks.note: a yaw is a turn about the vertical axis

explanation.surface: Turn north, they say, below the clearing to find the hill path.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ridgeway is an ancient track along the chalk downs of southern England.
explanation.definitionFit: A ridgeway is a road or track running along the crest of a ridge, hence a hilltop path.

clue.text: Philosopher with unusually deep pockets I bug

indicators.note: something done unusually departs from the normal order of its letters
to pocket something is to put it inside, enclosing it

blocks.note: John Stuart Mill, the English philosopher

explanation.surface: A wealthy thinker with unusually deep pockets pesters me.
explanation.walkthrough: Deep pockets suggests riches, but the philosopher-plus-anagram pockets the I.
explanation.definitionFit: A bug is loosely any creepy-crawly, so the many-legged millipede counts.

clue.text: Bad behaviour did seem wrong

indicators.note: letters that have gone wrong are out of their proper order

explanation.surface: Someone's bad behaviour certainly looked wrong.
explanation.definitionFit: A misdeed is a wrongful act, an example of behaving badly.

clue.text: Indian beggar had us at sixes and sevens

indicators.note: the idiom means in total confusion, so the letters are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: A mendicant in India left us thoroughly confused.
explanation.definitionFit: A sadhu is a Hindu holy man who renounces possessions and lives on alms, hence a religious mendicant.

clue.text: Messy university cleared out pens books and papers

indicators.note: a word cleared out has its insides emptied, leaving just the outer letters
to pen something is to enclose it, as livestock in a fold

blocks.note: New Testament, a set of books of the Bible

explanation.surface: A disorganised university emptied out its pens, books and papers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pens' looks like one of a list of stationery but is the enclosing verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Messy and untidy are straightforward synonyms describing disorder.

clue.text: Alternative way out of tunnel

indicators.note: taking something out of a word removes those letters from it

blocks.note: a subway is a pedestrian underpass
taken as written, the letters removed

explanation.surface: Looking for another exit from an underpass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Way out' sounds like an exit, but the word way is taken out of the tunnel; in Britain a subway is a pedestrian underpass.
explanation.definitionFit: A sub is a substitute, a replacement or stand-in for something else.

clue.text: Young Scot from Rhode Island brought up during Prohibition

indicators.note: in a down clue, brought up means raised so its letters read bottom to top
what happens during something sits inside its span

blocks.note: postal abbreviation for the US state

explanation.surface: A young Scotsman raised in Rhode Island in the Prohibition era.
explanation.walkthrough: Capital-P Prohibition suggests the US alcohol ban of the 1920s, but it is just any ban.
explanation.definitionFit: Bairn is the Scottish word for a child.

clue.text: Riders in Hackney tend to cycle for approval

indicators.note: Hackney is in the East End, where the Cockney accent drops the h
to cycle letters is to move one from the front round to the back
the word in places the riders inside the other word

explanation.surface: Cyclists in east London tend to ride their bikes to win approval.
explanation.walkthrough: Dropping the h from horsemen gives the Cockney 'orsemen; moving the T of tend to the back gives ENDT, which wraps around them.
explanation.definitionFit: An endorsement is a statement of support or sanction, a form of approval.

clue.text: Engineers take steps to put in new arrangement

blocks.note: Royal Engineers, the British army corps

explanation.surface: Army engineers act to reorganise things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take steps' sounds like taking action, but it means dancing.
explanation.definitionFit: To rejig is informal British for rearranging or reorganising something.

clue.text: Letter P among terrible tiles at end of Scrabble

indicators.note: something terrible is in a bad state, so the letters are messed up
the end of a word is its last letter
something placed among others sits in the middle of them

explanation.surface: A player is stuck with the letter P and a bad rack of tiles at the end of a Scrabble game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letter' sounds like a Scrabble tile, but it means a written message.
explanation.definitionFit: An epistle is a formal or literary letter, like those of the New Testament.

clue.text: Learner behind Beetle with Danish parts

definitions.note: a plural defining a single place name, fair because the peninsula is made up of several Danish regions

indicators.note: one thing behind another follows it, so it is placed after

blocks.note: to beetle is to overhang or project
from the L-plate on a learner's car

explanation.surface: A learner driver follows a VW Beetle with Danish components.
explanation.walkthrough: Capital-B Beetle suggests the Volkswagen car, but it is the verb meaning to stick out.
explanation.definitionFit: Jutland is the peninsula that forms mainland Denmark, comprising several regions of the country.

clue.text: Tree expert died meaning to eat last Rolo

indicators.note: something that eats takes food inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: the last of something is its end
taken as written: a Rolo is a chocolate-covered caramel sweet
the gist is the essential meaning

explanation.surface: A tree specialist died wanting to eat the last chocolate sweet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Meaning to' reads as 'intending to', but meaning is a word for its sense, wrapped with died around the last Rolo.
explanation.definitionFit: Dendrology is the scientific study of trees, so a dendrologist is a specialist in them.
